Here's a toast you can use. Swap in their names and a personal detail or two.

---

**Wedding Toast**

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [Your Name], [Bride]'s [brother/sister].

I've been thinking about how to describe these two, and I realized it's simple: they run toward the things everyone else runs away from.

[Bride], you're a nurse. You walk into the hardest days of people's lives and make them a little less scary. You hold hands, you stay calm, and you somehow find the right words when there aren't any. I've known you my whole life, and you've always been the person who takes care of everyone else.

[Groom], you're a firefighter. When everyone else is heading out of the building, you're the one heading in. I can't think of anyone better suited to love my sister, because she's spent her life caring for others and deserves someone who will always show up for her.

Between the two of you, you've got every emergency covered. Medical? Handled. Fire? Handled. The only thing neither of you can fix is who forgot to take out the trash, and I suspect that's where the real drama begins.

But seriously, you both spend your days taking care of strangers, often on their worst days. Tonight, you get to be on each other's best day. You've found someone who understands the long shifts, the missed dinners, and the weight of what you carry, and who will be waiting at the end of it with open arms.

So please raise your glasses.

To [Bride] and [Groom]: may your home always be calm, may your shifts always end safely, and may you always find your way back to each other.

Cheers!

---

If you tell me how you'd like it to sound (funnier, more sentimental, shorter) or share a story about the couple, I can tailor it.

# Wedding Toast

*Placeholders in [brackets]. Spoken, it runs about 2½ minutes.*

---

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [Name], [Bride]'s [older/younger] sister.

I've known [Bride] my whole life, and I can tell you she has always been the person who shows up. When I was sick, she was there. When I was heartbroken, she was there. [Insert one 15-second true story: the time she did something small and caring, like driving over with soup or staying on the phone until 2 a.m.] Nobody was surprised when she became a nurse. It was less a career choice than a confirmation.

Nurses are the people who are at their best when everyone else is at their worst. They're calm at 3 a.m. They notice the thing nobody said out loud. They hold a hand when there's nothing left to fix.

Then [Bride] met [Groom], a man who runs *toward* the things everyone else is running away from.

[Beat.]

I'll admit I wondered how two people with jobs like these would fit together. Then I saw them. She's the one who tells you, gently, what you need to hear. He's the one who carries you out when you can't walk. Between the two of them, nobody in this room has anything to worry about, **unless** there's a medical emergency during the cake-cutting. In that case, I'd say we're the best-covered wedding in the state.

[Optional joke, light and affectionate: *"[Groom] has rescued people from burning buildings. [Bride] has patched up the people who got rescued. The real test of their marriage will be who gets to be in charge when one of them has a cold."*]

What I love most is that both of them chose lives of service. Neither of them ever clocks out of caring. So tonight my wish for you is simple: **let someone take care of you, too.** [Bride], you've spent years looking after everyone else. [Groom], you've spent years racing to everyone else's worst day. In each other, you've finally found someone who looks after *you*, and who'll still be there when the shift ends.

I hope your home is the place where the alarms go quiet. May your love stay steady, your hearts strong, and your pulse a little fast every time the other walks in.

Everyone, please raise your glasses:

**To [Bride] and [Groom]: may your love burn bright without ever needing a rescue, and may it heal everything it touches. Cheers!**

---

## Making it land

- **Replace the story.** A specific memory (the soup, the late-night call) will do more than anything else in the toast. Keep it to 15–20 seconds and make it about her character, not an embarrassing prank.
- **Add one detail about him.** Something you've seen firsthand, like how he looks at her or how he treated your family the first time he met them. It shows you've accepted him, and it will get the best reaction.
- **Pause after the jokes.** Wait a full beat before the next line.
- **Keep the medical and fire jokes warm.** They should tease the job, not the people. Skip anything about injuries or tragedy, since some guests may have lost someone.
- **Hold the glass until the last line.** Don't raise it early, and make eye contact with the couple on "Cheers."
- **Practice out loud three times.** Aim for under 3 minutes. If you tear up, pause and breathe. It helps the toast.

## Wedding Toast

Good evening, everyone. I'm [MY NAME], [SISTER]'s sibling, which means I've known her longest and have the most dirt, and tonight I'm choosing mercy.

Let me tell you who my sister is. [STORY]

*(Placeholder: a 60–80 word story. Aim for one moment, one detail, and a punchline or a quiet beat at the end.)*

That's [SISTER]. She doesn't announce that she's taking care of you. She just starts doing it, and you find out later.

Which brings me to [SPOUSE]. When I thought about the two of them, I realized something. A nurse and a firefighter have the same job, just with different equipment.

Both of them stay calm when everyone around them isn't. Both of them show up at the hours the rest of us are asleep, or hiding, or hoping it's someone else's problem. And both of them spend their days caring for complete strangers, people they've never met and may never see again, on what is often the worst day of those people's lives. They don't ask for thanks. Mostly they ask, "Okay, what's going on? Let's figure it out."

I find that remarkable. I also find it a little unfair, because it means that in this marriage, nobody has ever once panicked about a household emergency. Burnt dinner? Handled. Leaking sink? Triage. I assume the smoke detector is just a conversation starter.

But here's what I really love. For all the people these two have looked after, it's wonderful to see them find someone who looks after *them*. [SISTER], you spend your life taking care of everyone else. [SPOUSE], you've got the same habit. Tonight, you both get to be the ones who are cared for.

So, everyone, please raise your glass. To [SISTER] and [SPOUSE]: may your shifts be quiet, your home be calm, and may you always be each other's safe place to land.

To the happy couple!

---

**Assumptions made**
- You're a sibling (I used "[SISTER]'s sibling" to avoid guessing). Swap in "brother," "sister," or "best friend" as appropriate.
- The couple is already married or marrying tonight, and the audience includes both families.
- I didn't specify the couple's genders beyond your sister, so [SPOUSE] is used throughout. Adjust pronouns if needed. The toast currently avoids them.
- The early line I return to is the "taking care of you" idea, closing with the couple as each other's safe place.
- The [STORY] slot is sized at about 70 words, which my count includes.

**Word count and timing**
- About 275 words with a 70-word story filled in.
- At a relaxed speaking pace of about 130 words per minute, this runs roughly 2 minutes, a bit longer with laughter pauses.

**What to send back:** a real memory of your sister. It will do the most to sharpen this. The story is the part only you can write, and it also lets me make the nurse-and-firefighter turn echo a specific trait of hers instead of a general one. How the couple met would help too, but the memory comes first.
